subject.name: Python & FastAPI
subject.description: Comprehensive interview preparation covering Python language fundamentals, object-oriented programming, typing, standard library, testing, performance, concurrency, and building production APIs with FastAPI.

topics.name: Python Fundamentals
topics.description: Syntax, variables, data types, operators, control flow, and basic language behavior.

topics.name: Strings, Collections & Comprehensions
topics.description: Strings, lists, tuples, dictionaries, sets, slicing, and comprehensions.

topics.name: Functions, Scope & Functional Features
topics.description: Function definitions, arguments, scope, closures, decorators, lambdas, and functional tools.

topics.name: Object-Oriented Programming
topics.description: Classes, objects, inheritance, composition, polymorphism, properties, and special methods.

topics.name: Exceptions & Error Handling
topics.description: Exception hierarchy, custom exceptions, handling strategies, and context managers.

topics.name: Modules, Packages & Environments
topics.description: Imports, packages, virtual environments, dependency management, and project organization.

topics.name: Iterators, Generators & Context Managers
topics.description: Iteration protocol, generators, yield, context management, and resource cleanup.

topics.name: Typing, Dataclasses & Modern Python
topics.description: Type hints, generics, protocols, dataclasses, enums, and modern Python features.

topics.name: Files, Serialization & Standard Library
topics.description: File operations, JSON, CSV, pathlib, logging, datetime, and useful standard-library modules.

topics.name: Concurrency, Asyncio & Multiprocessing
topics.description: Threads, processes, asyncio, coroutines, event loops, and concurrency trade-offs.

topics.name: Testing, Debugging & Code Quality
topics.description: pytest, unittest, mocking, debugging, linting, formatting, and maintainable code.

topics.name: Performance, Memory & Python Internals
topics.description: Big-O, profiling, memory behavior, garbage collection, GIL, and optimization.

topics.name: FastAPI Fundamentals & Application Setup
topics.description: FastAPI application structure, routing, path operations, ASGI, and application lifecycle.

topics.name: Pydantic, Validation & Data Models
topics.description: Request and response models, validation, serialization, field constraints, and Pydantic behavior.

topics.name: Dependency Injection & Application Architecture
topics.description: Depends, dependency scopes, reusable dependencies, app structure, and configuration.

topics.name: Async Endpoints & Background Tasks
topics.description: Async/await in endpoints, blocking work, background tasks, and concurrency considerations.

topics.name: Databases, SQLAlchemy & Persistence
topics.description: Database sessions, SQLAlchemy integration, transactions, repository patterns, and migrations.

topics.name: Authentication, Authorization & Security
topics.description: OAuth2 password flow, JWT concepts, password hashing, scopes, CORS, and security practices.

topics.name: Errors, Middleware & API Design
topics.description: Exception handlers, middleware, status codes, response models, pagination, and API contracts.

topics.name: Testing, Deployment & Production FastAPI
topics.description: TestClient, dependency overrides, lifespan, ASGI servers, containers, observability, and deployment.

questions.question: What is the purpose of declaring a FastAPI endpoint with `async def`?

options.text: Make CPU-heavy Python code automatically parallel
Run the endpoint in a new process
Allow the endpoint to await nonblocking asynchronous operations
Guarantee faster execution for every function

questions.explanation: Async endpoints can yield control while awaiting asynchronous I/O. They do not make blocking or CPU-bound code automatically nonblocking.

questions.question: What should an async endpoint use for a nonblocking HTTP request to another service?

options.text: A synchronous client called repeatedly in a tight loop

questions.explanation: An async-compatible client such as HTTPX's `AsyncClient` allows the event loop to manage concurrent network waits.

questions.question: What is the purpose of FastAPI's `BackgroundTasks`?

options.text: Schedule small tasks to run after the response is sent
Create durable distributed jobs with guaranteed retries
Run a task before request validation
Replace a message broker for all workloads

questions.explanation: BackgroundTasks are useful for lightweight post-response work. They are not a durable job queue and do not provide the guarantees of a dedicated worker system.

questions.question: Why should a CPU-intensive function not run directly on the asyncio event loop?

options.text: It automatically becomes a database transaction
It can block the event loop and prevent other coroutines from making progress
It is always slower than a thread
It cancels all other tasks permanently

questions.explanation: CPU-heavy synchronous work occupies the event-loop thread. Use a process pool or separate worker for CPU-bound workloads when parallelism is required.

questions.question: What does `await` require in Python?

options.text: An awaitable object, such as a coroutine, Task, or Future

questions.explanation: `await` is used with awaitables. A normal synchronous function result cannot simply be awaited.

questions.question: What is the practical difference between a synchronous `def` endpoint and an `async def` endpoint in FastAPI?

options.text: Both always run in separate processes
A def endpoint cannot use dependencies
An async endpoint always uses a thread pool
FastAPI runs normal def path operations in a thread pool, while async def path operations run on the event loop

questions.explanation: FastAPI offloads normal synchronous path operations to a thread pool so blocking work does not directly block the event loop. Async endpoints should use nonblocking operations or explicitly offload blocking work.

questions.question: When is FastAPI's `BackgroundTasks` not an adequate solution?

options.text: When work needs durable delivery, retries, scheduling, or execution independent of the web process
When sending a small best-effort email after a response

questions.explanation: For durable or resource-intensive jobs, use a task queue or worker architecture such as Celery, RQ, Dramatiq, or a broker-backed worker.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an async context manager for an HTTP client?

options.text: Ensure the client is closed after its asynchronous use
Persist response data to SQL automatically

questions.explanation: Async context managers support deterministic acquisition and cleanup of asynchronous resources, for example `async with AsyncClient() as client`.

questions.question: Why should an application avoid creating a new HTTP client for every outbound request?

options.text: HTTP clients cannot be instantiated more than once
It prevents effective connection pooling and adds connection setup overhead

questions.explanation: Reusing a properly managed client allows connection pooling and resource reuse. Manage the client lifecycle at application scope where appropriate.

questions.question: What is a common strategy for isolating a blocking library call inside an async FastAPI workflow?

options.text: Call it directly and assume asyncio detects blocking code
Wrap it in `async def` without changing the call
Run it in a worker thread or process using an appropriate offloading mechanism

questions.explanation: Declaring a function async does not make its internal blocking calls nonblocking. Offload blocking I/O to a thread and CPU-heavy work to a process or external worker, as appropriate.

questions.question: What is authentication?

options.text: Determining whether a caller can access a specific resource
Verifying the identity of a caller

questions.explanation: Authentication establishes who the caller is. Authorization determines what that identity is allowed to do.

questions.question: What is authorization?

options.text: Determining what an authenticated identity is permitted to access or perform

questions.explanation: Authorization evaluates permissions, roles, or scopes for a requested operation or resource.

questions.question: Why should passwords not be stored as plaintext?

options.text: A database leak would expose users' original passwords directly
Passwords must be stored in JWT payloads

questions.explanation: Store passwords using a dedicated password-hashing algorithm with salts and appropriate work factors. Never store or log plaintext passwords.

questions.question: What is a JWT commonly used for in an API?

options.text: Represent signed claims that can be presented as an access token
Store server-side session state by default

questions.explanation: A JWT can carry claims and be signed so a resource server can validate its integrity. A signed JWT is not necessarily encrypted.

questions.question: What does CORS control?

options.text: Which users can query the database
Which browser origins are allowed to make cross-origin requests under the browser's CORS policy

questions.explanation: CORS is a browser-enforced cross-origin resource sharing mechanism. It is not authentication or authorization and does not prevent non-browser clients from calling an API.

questions.question: What is the role of `OAuth2PasswordBearer` in FastAPI?

options.text: Validate a JWT signature automatically in every configuration
Create a user in the database
Extract a bearer token from the Authorization header and integrate the OAuth2 password flow scheme into dependencies and OpenAPI

questions.explanation: `OAuth2PasswordBearer` extracts the bearer token and declares an OAuth2 security scheme. Token verification, user lookup, and authorization logic still need to be implemented.

questions.question: What should a JWT resource server validate?

options.text: Signature and relevant claims such as issuer, audience, expiration, and allowed algorithms
Only that the token has three segments

questions.explanation: A JWT payload is not trusted simply because it can be decoded. Verify signature and enforce issuer, audience, expiration, and algorithm policy appropriate to the system.

questions.question: Why is password hashing with a purpose-built algorithm such as Argon2 or bcrypt preferred over plain SHA-256?

options.text: Password hashing algorithms are designed to make large-scale guessing expensive through configurable work factors and salts

questions.explanation: General-purpose hashes are too fast for password storage. Use a password hashing/KDF algorithm with salts and suitable cost parameters, following current security guidance.

questions.question: What is the purpose of OAuth2 scopes?

options.text: Represent granular permissions associated with an access token

questions.explanation: Scopes express permissions such as `orders:read` or `orders:write`, allowing APIs to enforce fine-grained authorization.

questions.question: Why should an API avoid trusting user IDs or roles supplied directly in request bodies for authorization decisions?

options.text: Request bodies are always encrypted by FastAPI
Clients can alter request data, so authorization must be based on verified identity and trusted server-side policy

questions.explanation: Authorization must derive from authenticated principal information and server-side ownership/permission checks. User-provided fields are untrusted input.

questions.question: What is SQLAlchemy commonly used for in a FastAPI application?

options.text: Database access through SQL expression and ORM capabilities

questions.explanation: SQLAlchemy provides SQL toolkit and ORM functionality. FastAPI does not mandate a particular database library.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a database session in SQLAlchemy?

options.text: Represent a unit of work for interacting with the database and tracking ORM changes
Store user login sessions in the browser

questions.explanation: A Session manages ORM identity state and transaction interaction. It should have a deliberate lifecycle and should not be shared indiscriminately across concurrent requests.

questions.question: Why should a database session generally be closed or otherwise cleaned up after request processing?

options.text: To release connection and transactional resources back to the pool

questions.explanation: A session dependency commonly yields a session and closes it in cleanup, ensuring resources are not leaked.

questions.question: What is a database migration?

options.text: A copy of an API response
A versioned change to database schema or data structure

questions.explanation: Migrations record and apply schema changes over time. Alembic is commonly used with SQLAlchemy.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a repository layer in a backend application?

options.text: Encapsulate data access operations behind an application-facing interface

questions.explanation: A repository can isolate persistence details from business logic. It is a design choice, not a mandatory FastAPI feature.

questions.question: Why should a SQLAlchemy Session generally not be shared across concurrent requests or asyncio tasks?

options.text: It is an immutable global singleton
It is mutable unit-of-work state and is not designed for unrestricted concurrent use
It can only execute SELECT queries

questions.explanation: A Session tracks identity-map and transaction state and is not safe for concurrent use. Use one session per request/task unit of work; async applications use the appropriate AsyncSession pattern.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `commit()` in a SQLAlchemy session?
questions.explanation: `commit()` flushes pending changes and commits the current transaction. If a transaction fails, the session usually needs rollback before reuse.

questions.question: What is the difference between `flush()` and `commit()`?

options.text: Flush closes the session; commit keeps it open
Flush rolls back changes; commit validates Pydantic
Flush sends pending changes to the database within the current transaction; commit makes the transaction durable

questions.explanation: A flush synchronizes pending ORM changes with the database but does not commit the transaction. Commit finalizes the transaction.

questions.question: What is Alembic used for?

options.text: Database schema migration management, commonly with SQLAlchemy

questions.explanation: Alembic tracks schema changes through migration scripts that can be applied and rolled back in controlled deployment workflows.

questions.question: Why is it often preferable to keep database transactions short in web APIs?

options.text: Long transactions hold resources and locks longer, increasing contention and reducing throughput

questions.explanation: Transactions should cover the atomic business operation without unnecessary network waits or long-running work. This limits lock duration and connection occupancy.

questions.question: Which test client is commonly used to test FastAPI endpoints without starting a real network server?
questions.explanation: `TestClient` provides an HTTPX/Starlette-based interface for making requests against the ASGI application in tests.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `pytest` in a FastAPI project?

options.text: Run automated tests and provide fixtures, parametrization, and assertions

questions.explanation: Pytest is a popular test runner and framework for unit and integration tests in Python projects.

questions.question: What does a health endpoint commonly communicate?

options.text: Whether the application or selected dependencies are healthy
The source code version of every dependency

questions.explanation: Health endpoints support monitoring and orchestration. Liveness and readiness should be designed to answer different operational questions.

questions.question: What is Docker commonly used for when deploying a FastAPI service?

options.text: Package the application and its runtime dependencies into a container image

questions.explanation: A container image packages the application and required runtime layers so it can run consistently in supported container environments.

questions.question: What is the role of an ASGI server in production?

options.text: Accept network connections and run the ASGI application

questions.explanation: An ASGI server such as Uvicorn or Hypercorn hosts the application and handles the server protocol interface.

questions.question: How can a FastAPI test replace the real database dependency with a test implementation?

options.text: Edit the production database connection at runtime

questions.explanation: Dependency overrides make it possible to inject a test session or fake repository without changing the endpoint implementation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of FastAPI's lifespan mechanism?

options.text: Manage application startup and shutdown resources such as clients and connection pools

questions.explanation: Lifespan handlers provide startup and shutdown logic for application-scoped resources. They are a good place to initialize and close long-lived clients or pools.

questions.question: Why should secrets be injected through environment or secret-management systems rather than committed in source code?

options.text: Committed secrets can leak through source control, build artifacts, and developer copies
Environment variables are automatically encrypted in all deployments

questions.explanation: Use secret managers or secure deployment-time injection. If a secret is exposed, rotate it; deleting it from the latest commit does not remove repository history.

questions.question: What is a common reason to run multiple worker processes for a FastAPI service?

options.text: Share one in-memory Python object across all workers
Use multiple processes to handle concurrent requests and utilize multiple CPU cores
Make all endpoints execute in one event loop

questions.explanation: Multiple workers can use multiple cores and improve throughput, but each process has its own memory and resource pools. Capacity planning must account for total database connections and memory.

questions.question: Why is in-memory state in a FastAPI process unreliable for shared application state in a multi-worker deployment?

options.text: FastAPI deletes all global variables after each request
Uvicorn converts global state to SQL automatically
Each worker has separate process memory, so updates are not automatically shared across workers

questions.explanation: Workers are separate processes. Shared state that must be consistent across workers or instances belongs in an external system such as a database, cache, or message broker.

questions.question: Which function is commonly used to declare a FastAPI dependency?
questions.explanation: `Depends` declares a dependency that FastAPI resolves when invoking a path operation or another dependency.

questions.question: What can a FastAPI dependency provide to an endpoint?

options.text: Reusable values or services such as a database session, current user, or configuration

questions.explanation: Dependencies can encapsulate reusable logic, resources, and authorization checks, and can themselves depend on other dependencies.

questions.question: How is a dependency commonly declared in a path operation parameter?
questions.explanation: FastAPI calls the dependency and injects its result into the endpoint parameter.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `APIRouter`?

options.text: Group related path operations into reusable routers that can be included in an application

questions.explanation: `APIRouter` helps organize endpoints by feature or resource and can apply prefixes, tags, dependencies, and response configuration.

questions.question: Why is separating routers, schemas, services, and repositories useful?

options.text: It creates clearer boundaries between HTTP handling, validation, business logic, and data access
It removes the need for tests

questions.explanation: Layered organization helps maintainability and testability. The exact architecture should match project complexity rather than follow a rigid folder count.

questions.question: What is dependency caching behavior in a typical FastAPI request?

options.text: Dependencies are cached forever across all users
The same dependency is generally called once per request and its result reused for repeated dependency declarations unless caching is disabled
Every dependency is executed in a separate process

questions.explanation: FastAPI normally caches dependency results within a request. `use_cache=False` can request a fresh resolution for a particular dependency declaration.

questions.question: How can a dependency be overridden in a FastAPI test?

options.text: Edit the dependency source file before every test
Set a global environment variable only
Use `app.dependency_overrides` to map the original dependency to a test dependency

questions.explanation: FastAPI exposes a dependency override mapping that allows tests to replace database, authentication, or external-service dependencies.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a dependency that uses `yield`?

options.text: Provide setup and teardown around the request's use of a resource

questions.explanation: A yield dependency can acquire a resource before yielding it and perform cleanup afterward, commonly for database sessions. Scope and lifecycle details depend on FastAPI version and dependency configuration.

questions.question: What is a good practice for sharing application-wide configuration in FastAPI?

options.text: Load and validate settings through a dedicated settings object and provide it through a controlled dependency or app state
Read environment variables independently in every endpoint
Store configuration in request query parameters

questions.explanation: A centralized settings model makes configuration consistent and testable. Secrets should come from secure environment or secret-management mechanisms, not source control.

questions.question: Why can creating a database engine or network client at module import time complicate testing and application lifecycle?

options.text: Python does not allow global objects
It creates side effects during import and can make resource initialization, cleanup, and test isolation harder to control
FastAPI cannot import modules with classes

questions.explanation: Managing resources through application lifespan or a deliberate provider makes startup/shutdown explicit and simplifies test setup and cleanup.

questions.question: What is FastAPI?

options.text: A Python framework for building APIs using standard Python type hints

questions.explanation: FastAPI is a modern Python web framework for APIs. It uses type hints and integrates with Pydantic for data validation and OpenAPI documentation.

questions.question: Which ASGI server is commonly used to run a FastAPI application locally?
questions.explanation: Uvicorn is a commonly used ASGI server for running FastAPI. Production deployments may use Uvicorn workers or another ASGI server configuration.

questions.question: How is a basic FastAPI application instance commonly created?
questions.explanation: The `FastAPI` class creates the application object to which path operations, middleware, exception handlers, and lifecycle configuration are attached.

questions.question: Which decorator defines a GET endpoint in FastAPI?
questions.explanation: FastAPI provides decorators such as `@app.get`, `@app.post`, `@app.put`, and `@app.delete` to register path operations.

questions.question: What is an ASGI application?

options.text: An application interface designed for asynchronous-capable Python web servers and frameworks

questions.explanation: ASGI is the asynchronous successor/interface alongside WSGI, supporting HTTP and other protocols with async application call semantics.

questions.question: What is the purpose of FastAPI's automatic OpenAPI schema generation?

options.text: Describe API paths, parameters, request bodies, responses, and schemas for documentation and tooling

questions.explanation: FastAPI derives an OpenAPI schema from path operations, dependencies, and Pydantic models. This powers interactive docs and client-generation tooling.

questions.question: What are the default interactive API documentation routes in a typical FastAPI app?

options.text: `/docs` for Swagger UI and `/redoc` for ReDoc

questions.explanation: A typical FastAPI application exposes Swagger UI at `/docs`, ReDoc at `/redoc`, and the OpenAPI JSON schema at `/openapi.json`, unless configured otherwise.

questions.question: What is the difference between a path parameter and a query parameter?

options.text: A path parameter is always JSON; a query parameter is always a header
They are parsed only by the database
A path parameter is part of the URL path; a query parameter follows the `?` in the URL

questions.explanation: For `/users/{user_id}`, `user_id` is a path parameter. In `/users?active=true`, `active` is a query parameter.

questions.question: What does FastAPI generally use to infer a request body model?

options.text: A Pydantic model type declared as a path operation parameter
A variable name beginning with `body_` only
A SQLAlchemy model in every case

questions.explanation: A Pydantic model parameter is interpreted as request body data and validated before the endpoint function receives it.

questions.question: What is the key difference between WSGI and ASGI relevant to FastAPI?

options.text: WSGI supports Python but ASGI supports Java
ASGI supports asynchronous application execution and protocols such as WebSockets, while traditional WSGI is synchronous

questions.explanation: FastAPI is built for ASGI, enabling async request handling and protocols such as WebSockets. WSGI has a synchronous callable interface.

questions.question: How do you return an HTTP error from a FastAPI endpoint?

options.text: Raise `HTTPException` with an appropriate status code and detail

questions.explanation: FastAPI's `HTTPException` is raised to terminate the request with a specified HTTP status and detail payload.

questions.question: What is middleware in a FastAPI application?

options.text: Code that can process requests and responses around the application

questions.explanation: Middleware wraps request/response processing and is useful for cross-cutting concerns such as request IDs, timing, and headers.

questions.question: Which status code is commonly used when a resource is successfully created?
questions.explanation: 201 Created indicates successful resource creation and may include a Location header pointing to the new resource.

questions.question: Which status code indicates that the caller is not authenticated or has not supplied valid authentication credentials?
questions.explanation: 401 indicates missing or invalid authentication credentials. 403 generally means the caller is authenticated but not permitted to perform the operation.

questions.question: What is the purpose of pagination in a collection endpoint?

options.text: Limit response size and support retrieval of large result sets in manageable portions

questions.explanation: Pagination improves API usability and controls query and payload sizes. Stable ordering is important; cursor pagination can help with large or changing datasets.

questions.question: How can an application register a custom exception handler in FastAPI?

options.text: Use `app.exception_handler(ExceptionType)` as a decorator or register a handler explicitly
Add the exception to a Pydantic model

questions.explanation: FastAPI supports exception handlers that translate specific exception types into consistent HTTP responses.

questions.question: What is a common purpose of request ID middleware?

options.text: Generate a primary key for every database table
Attach or propagate a correlation identifier so logs for one request can be related

questions.explanation: A correlation or request ID helps connect logs and traces across the request lifecycle and downstream services. Avoid trusting arbitrary IDs without validation or policy.

questions.question: Why should an API return a stable error response schema?

options.text: It makes every request return status 200
It removes the need for server logs
Clients can handle errors consistently without depending on internal exception text or implementation details

questions.explanation: A consistent error contract improves client integration and allows internal implementation to change without breaking consumers.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a response status code such as 204 No Content?

options.text: Indicate successful processing with no response body
Indicate that the server is unavailable
Indicate that the resource was created with a body

questions.explanation: 204 indicates successful completion without a response body. Clients should not expect a JSON response payload.

questions.question: Why should middleware be used selectively for business logic?

options.text: Middleware is cross-cutting and often lacks resource-specific context; business rules are usually clearer in dependencies or service-layer code
Middleware always runs after the response is sent
FastAPI middleware is only for static files

questions.explanation: Middleware is appropriate for concerns spanning requests. Domain authorization and business workflows are generally easier to test and reason about in explicit dependencies and services.

questions.question: What role does Pydantic play in a typical FastAPI application?

options.text: Define data models and validate/serialize input and output data

questions.explanation: FastAPI integrates closely with Pydantic models for parsing, validation, and schema generation.

questions.question: How do you declare a Pydantic model field as an integer?

options.text: Annotate it with `int` in a `BaseModel` subclass

questions.explanation: Pydantic models use Python annotations to describe field types and validate input data accordingly.

questions.question: What happens when a request body fails FastAPI's normal validation?

options.text: FastAPI returns a 422 validation error response by default

questions.explanation: FastAPI validates request data before calling the path operation. Validation failures are normally returned as HTTP 422 with structured details.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `response_model` on a FastAPI path operation?

options.text: Define the database transaction isolation level
Validate, document, and serialize the response according to a declared schema

questions.explanation: `response_model` defines the public response schema and helps filter/serialize returned data, which can prevent accidental exposure of internal fields.

questions.question: How can a Pydantic field be made optional in a model?

options.text: Use a union with None, such as `str | None`, and provide a default when appropriate

questions.explanation: A type such as `str | None` allows None as a value. In Pydantic v2, whether the field is required is distinct from whether it accepts None; a default such as `= None` makes it non-required.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `Field()` in Pydantic?

options.text: Add field metadata, constraints, aliases, defaults, and schema information

questions.explanation: `Field` can define constraints such as minimum length, descriptions, aliases, and other schema metadata. Exact constraint APIs depend on the Pydantic version.

questions.question: What is the difference between a request model and a response model?

options.text: A request model defines accepted input; a response model defines the public output contract
A request model is always a database entity; a response model is always a DTO

questions.explanation: Separate models allow input validation and output exposure to evolve independently, helping prevent clients from setting server-controlled fields or seeing sensitive data.

questions.question: What is Pydantic's `model_dump()` used for in Pydantic v2?

options.text: Convert a model into a Python dictionary representation

questions.explanation: `model_dump()` returns a dictionary representation and supports options for aliases, excluded fields, and serialization behavior. `model_dump_json()` returns JSON text.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a Pydantic field validator?

options.text: Apply custom validation or transformation logic to a field's value

questions.explanation: Field validators provide custom rules for individual fields. Model validators can enforce rules involving multiple fields.

questions.question: Why should a Pydantic model not automatically be treated as a trusted domain entity?

options.text: Pydantic models are always mutable database rows
It validates an external data shape, but domain invariants and authorization rules may require separate application logic

questions.explanation: Request models protect the API boundary. Business rules, authorization, and persistence invariants belong in appropriate application/domain layers and must not rely solely on request parsing.

questions.question: Which Python collection is ordered and mutable?
questions.explanation: Lists preserve order and can be modified after creation. Tuples and strings are immutable; frozensets are immutable sets.

questions.question: Which collection is typically used to store unique elements?
questions.explanation: A set stores distinct hashable elements and supports efficient membership checks on average.

questions.question: How do you access the first element of a list named `items`?
questions.explanation: Python sequences use zero-based indexing, so index 0 refers to the first element. `items[-0]` is also index 0, but is not the usual expression.

questions.question: Which syntax creates a tuple containing one element?
questions.explanation: The trailing comma makes it a one-element tuple. Parentheses alone do not create a tuple; `(5)` is just the integer 5.

questions.question: Which method adds one element to the end of a list?
questions.explanation: `list.append(value)` adds one item at the end. `extend` adds elements from an iterable.

questions.question: What does the slice `values[1:4]` return?
questions.explanation: The start index is included and the stop index is excluded. Slicing creates a new list for a list input.

questions.question: What is a dictionary key required to be?
questions.explanation: Dictionary keys must be hashable so Python can compute a stable hash. Common keys include strings, numbers, and tuples of hashable values.

questions.question: What is the main difference between `list.sort()` and `sorted(list_value)`?

options.text: `sorted()` modifies the original list; `sort()` returns a new list
`list.sort()` modifies the list in place; `sorted()` returns a new sorted list
Both always return the same new list

questions.explanation: `list.sort()` sorts the list in place and returns `None`. `sorted()` accepts an iterable and returns a new list.

questions.question: What does a list comprehension produce?

options.text: A generator that can only be consumed once
A new list built by evaluating an expression for each item in an iterable

questions.explanation: A list comprehension creates a list. Generator expressions use parentheses and produce values lazily.

questions.question: Why can a tuple be used as a dictionary key only when its contents are hashable?

options.text: Python hashes only the first tuple element
A tuple's hashability depends on the hashability of all its elements

questions.explanation: A tuple is hashable only if all its elements are hashable. A tuple containing a list, for example, cannot be used as a dictionary key.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of `async def` in Python?

options.text: Define a coroutine function that can be awaited
Make every statement execute in parallel

questions.explanation: Calling an async function produces a coroutine object. It must be awaited or scheduled on an event loop to execute.

questions.question: What does `await` do inside a coroutine?

options.text: Converts a function to a generator permanently
Suspends the coroutine until an awaitable produces a result, allowing other tasks to run

questions.explanation: `await` yields control to the event loop while the awaited operation is pending, enabling cooperative concurrency.

questions.question: Which module provides Python's standard asynchronous I/O framework?
questions.explanation: `asyncio` provides event loops, tasks, futures, and coroutine scheduling for asynchronous I/O workloads.

questions.question: What is a thread commonly useful for in Python?

options.text: Guaranteeing CPU-bound Python bytecode runs on all cores under the standard GIL build
Overlapping I/O-bound work such as network or file operations

questions.explanation: Threads can overlap blocking I/O operations. Under conventional CPython builds with the GIL, CPU-bound Python bytecode generally does not scale across threads in the same way as multiprocessing.

questions.question: What is multiprocessing commonly used for?

options.text: Sharing one Python stack across all tasks
Running CPU-bound work in separate processes that can execute on multiple CPU cores

questions.explanation: Multiprocessing uses separate processes and can achieve CPU parallelism, with additional overhead for process startup and data transfer.

questions.question: What is the Global Interpreter Lock (GIL) in conventional CPython builds?

options.text: A lock that prevents multiple processes from running
A lock used only by asyncio
A lock that historically allows only one thread at a time to execute Python bytecode within an interpreter

questions.explanation: The GIL has historically constrained CPU-bound parallel execution of Python threads in standard CPython builds. Free-threaded builds and other Python implementations change this landscape.

questions.question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?

options.text: Concurrency is managing overlapping tasks; parallelism is executing tasks at the same time
Concurrency requires multiple CPU cores; parallelism does not
Parallelism is only possible with asyncio

questions.explanation: Concurrency concerns structuring multiple tasks so they make progress over overlapping periods. Parallelism means tasks execute simultaneously, often on multiple cores.

questions.question: What does `asyncio.gather()` commonly do?

options.text: Schedule or await multiple awaitables and collect their results
Convert a list into a thread-safe queue
Run synchronous code in a database transaction

questions.explanation: `asyncio.gather` runs awaitables concurrently and returns their results in input order when they complete successfully, subject to its exception behavior and options.

questions.question: Why is calling a blocking function directly inside an async endpoint problematic?

options.text: It automatically creates a background task
It turns the endpoint into a synchronous endpoint
It blocks the event-loop thread and delays other coroutines on that loop

questions.explanation: Blocking work prevents the event loop from scheduling other tasks while the call is running. Use async-compatible libraries or isolate blocking work in a thread/process executor as appropriate.

questions.question: When is multiprocessing generally a better fit than asyncio?

options.text: For waiting on thousands of nonblocking sockets
For simple sequential file reads only
For CPU-bound work that benefits from executing on multiple cores

questions.explanation: Multiprocessing can distribute CPU-intensive computations across processes. Asyncio is particularly effective for high-concurrency I/O when libraries support nonblocking operations.

questions.question: Which block is used to handle an exception in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses `try` with one or more `except` clauses to handle exceptions.

questions.question: What does the `finally` block do?

options.text: Runs only when no exception occurs
Runs cleanup code whether or not an exception occurred

questions.explanation: `finally` is intended for cleanup and normally executes whether the try block succeeds or fails.

questions.question: Which exception is raised when a dictionary key is not found using indexing?
questions.explanation: Dictionary subscription with a missing key raises `KeyError`. `dict.get()` can be used when a default value is preferable.

questions.question: Which exception is commonly raised when converting an invalid string to an integer?
questions.explanation: `int('abc')` raises `ValueError` because the argument has the right general type but an invalid value for conversion.

questions.question: What does `raise` do?
questions.explanation: `raise` triggers an exception. It can raise a new exception or re-raise the currently handled exception with a bare `raise`.

questions.question: Why should exception handlers generally catch specific exception types rather than use a bare `except`?

options.text: Specific handlers avoid accidentally swallowing unrelated failures and make recovery behavior clearer

questions.explanation: A bare except also catches system-exiting exceptions such as KeyboardInterrupt. Catch only errors the code can meaningfully handle.

questions.question: What does `raise NewError() from original_error` provide?

options.text: A retry of the original operation
A way to ignore the original error
Explicit exception chaining that preserves the underlying cause
A way to convert the exception to a warning

questions.explanation: Exception chaining records the causal relationship and helps diagnostics distinguish a high-level failure from its underlying cause.

questions.question: What is a custom exception commonly based on?
questions.explanation: Application-specific exceptions typically subclass `Exception` or a more specific built-in exception class.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a context manager when working with files?

options.text: Ensure the file is closed when the managed block exits
Keep the file open for the entire process
Convert the file into a generator

questions.explanation: The `with` statement invokes context-manager methods so resources can be reliably acquired and released, including when exceptions occur.

questions.question: Why is catching `Exception` at a process boundary sometimes appropriate but risky deep inside business logic?

options.text: Exception can only be caught in main()
A top-level boundary can log and translate unexpected failures, while broad inner catches may hide bugs or break error semantics
It guarantees that no error is lost
It converts all exceptions to checked exceptions

questions.explanation: Broad catches may be useful at a boundary that logs, reports, and safely terminates or responds. Inside business logic, catch only failures with a defined recovery path.

questions.question: Which mode opens a file for reading text?
questions.explanation: `r` opens an existing file for reading. `w` truncates or creates, `a` appends, and `x` creates exclusively.

questions.question: Why is `with open(path) as file:` preferred?

options.text: It ensures the file is closed when the block exits
It reads the whole file into a list

questions.explanation: The file object is a context manager. The `with` block closes it reliably, including when an exception occurs.

questions.question: Which standard library module is commonly used to work with JSON?
questions.explanation: The `json` module provides `dump`, `dumps`, `load`, and `loads` for JSON serialization and parsing.

questions.question: Which module provides an object-oriented interface for filesystem paths?
questions.explanation: `pathlib.Path` provides convenient path manipulation and filesystem operations across platforms.

questions.question: Which standard library module is commonly used to read and write CSV files?
questions.explanation: The `csv` module provides readers, writers, and dictionary-based helpers for CSV data.

questions.question: What is the difference between `json.dumps()` and `json.dump()`?

options.text: `dump()` returns a string; `dumps()` writes to a file
`dumps()` returns a JSON string; `dump()` writes JSON to a file-like object
Both write only to standard output

questions.explanation: `dumps` serializes to a string; `dump` serializes to a file-like object.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Python's `logging` module?

options.text: Provide configurable application logging with levels, handlers, and formatters
Automatically send logs to a cloud provider

questions.explanation: The logging module supports levels, handlers, formatters, and logger hierarchies, allowing output to be routed to files, streams, or integrations.

questions.question: What does `datetime.now()` return when called without a timezone argument?

options.text: A UTC-aware datetime in every environment
A naive datetime representing the local system time

questions.explanation: Without a timezone argument, `datetime.now()` returns a naive datetime. For timezone-aware application logic, use explicit timezone information such as `datetime.now(timezone.utc)`.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `argparse`?

options.text: Parse command-line arguments for Python programs

questions.explanation: `argparse` supports command-line options, positional arguments, help messages, and validation of CLI input.

questions.question: Why is `pickle` unsafe for untrusted input?

options.text: Unpickling can execute arbitrary code during deserialization

questions.explanation: Pickle is Python-specific and deserialization can invoke constructors or other callables. Never unpickle data from untrusted sources; prefer safer formats such as JSON for interchange.

questions.question: Which keyword defines a function in Python?
questions.explanation: `def` begins a function definition. `lambda` creates a small anonymous function expression.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a `return` statement?

options.text: Print a value to the terminal
Send a result back to the caller and end the function execution
Pause the function until the next call

questions.explanation: `return` exits the current function and optionally provides a value. A function without an explicit return yields `None`.

questions.question: What does `*args` collect in a function definition?

options.text: Extra keyword arguments as a dictionary
Extra positional arguments as a tuple

questions.explanation: `*args` gathers additional positional arguments into a tuple.

questions.question: What does `**kwargs` collect in a function definition?

options.text: Extra positional arguments as a list
Extra keyword arguments as a dictionary

questions.explanation: `**kwargs` gathers additional keyword arguments into a dictionary.

questions.question: What is a lambda expression in Python?
questions.explanation: A lambda creates a function from a single expression and is often used for short callbacks or sort keys.

questions.question: Why are mutable default arguments such as `def f(items=[])` often a bug?

options.text: Python copies the list on every call
The same list object is reused across calls when the default is not supplied

questions.explanation: Default argument expressions are evaluated once when the function is defined. Use `None` as a sentinel and create a new list inside the function when needed.

questions.question: What does the `nonlocal` keyword do?

options.text: Allows assignment to a variable in an enclosing function scope
Imports a name from another module

questions.explanation: `nonlocal` binds a name to the nearest enclosing function scope in which it is defined.

questions.question: What is a closure?

options.text: A function that always returns None
A module that cannot be imported
A function that retains access to variables from its enclosing lexical scope

questions.explanation: A closure captures references to variables from an enclosing scope, even after that outer function has returned.

questions.question: What does a decorator commonly do?

options.text: Wrap or transform a function or class to add behavior
Convert Python code to machine code
Make a function run in a separate process

questions.explanation: A decorator takes a callable or class and returns a replacement, often wrapping behavior such as logging, authorization, caching, or timing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `functools.wraps` inside a decorator?

options.text: Preserve important metadata from the wrapped function

questions.explanation: `functools.wraps` copies metadata such as the name, docstring, and annotations and sets `__wrapped__`, improving introspection and documentation.

questions.question: Which statement best describes Python?

options.text: A high-level, general-purpose programming language with a dynamic type system
A language that runs only in web browsers

questions.explanation: Python is a general-purpose language with dynamic typing and a broad ecosystem. It is commonly used for backend services, automation, data work, scripting, and many other domains.

questions.question: Which built-in type represents a whole number in Python?
questions.explanation: The `int` type represents integers. Python integers have arbitrary precision subject to available memory.

questions.question: What is the result of `type(3.5)`?
questions.explanation: A decimal-point numeric literal such as `3.5` is a Python `float`, typically implemented using double-precision floating-point.

questions.question: Which value represents the absence of a value in Python?
questions.explanation: `None` is Python's singleton value commonly used to represent absence or no result. Python does not use JavaScript's `null` keyword.

questions.question: Which operator performs integer floor division?
questions.explanation: `//` performs floor division. Unlike `/`, it rounds the quotient down toward negative infinity, which matters for negative operands.

questions.question: What is the result of `bool([])`?
questions.explanation: Empty containers are falsey in Python. Non-empty lists, tuples, dictionaries, and sets are truthy.

questions.question: What does the `is` operator test?

options.text: Whether two objects have equal values
Whether two objects have the same type
Whether two references point to the same object
Whether one value is contained in another

questions.explanation: `is` tests object identity. Use `==` to compare values. Identity checks are commonly appropriate for singletons such as `None`.

questions.question: What does `enumerate(items)` commonly provide when iterating over a sequence?

options.text: A sorted copy of the sequence
A dictionary mapping items to indexes
Pairs containing an index and the corresponding item

questions.explanation: `enumerate` yields index-item pairs and avoids manually maintaining a counter.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `pass` statement?

options.text: It is a no-operation placeholder statement
It skips to the next loop iteration

questions.explanation: `pass` performs no action and is useful where Python syntax requires a statement but implementation is intentionally empty.

questions.question: What does Python's LEGB rule describe?

options.text: The order in which modules are installed
The order used to resolve names: Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in

questions.explanation: LEGB describes lexical name lookup across local, enclosing function, global module, and built-in scopes.

questions.question: What is an iterable?

options.text: An object that can provide an iterator, commonly through `iter()`
An object that must be a list
A function that always returns a string
An object that can only be used once

questions.explanation: An iterable can be passed to `iter()` to obtain an iterator. Lists, tuples, strings, dictionaries, and generators are common examples.

questions.question: What does `next(iterator)` do?

options.text: Requests the next item from an iterator
Converts the iterator to a list

questions.explanation: `next()` asks an iterator for another value. When exhausted, the iterator raises `StopIteration`.

questions.question: Which keyword makes a function produce a generator?
questions.explanation: `yield` suspends a generator function and produces a value. Execution can resume later from the suspended point.

questions.question: What is a key characteristic of a generator?

options.text: It always stores all values in memory
It can be iterated only through indexing
It executes in a separate process
It produces values lazily as they are requested

questions.explanation: Generators are iterators that compute values on demand, often reducing memory usage for large or streaming data.

questions.question: Which statement begins a context-managed block?
questions.explanation: `with` invokes a context manager's enter and exit protocol and ensures exit handling when the block ends.

questions.question: What is the difference between an iterator and an iterable?

options.text: An iterator must be a dictionary; an iterable must be a list
An iterable can produce an iterator; an iterator maintains iteration state and implements `__next__`
An iterable can only be used once; an iterator can be reused
They are exactly the same protocol

questions.explanation: An iterator implements `__iter__` returning itself and `__next__` to produce values. An iterable need only provide an iterator.

questions.question: What happens when a generator function reaches `return`?

options.text: The generator finishes and raises StopIteration to its caller

questions.explanation: Returning from a generator ends iteration. A return value may be carried as the StopIteration value, though normal for-loops ignore it.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `contextlib.contextmanager`?

options.text: Convert any function into an async function
Cache the output of a generator
Allow a generator function to define a context manager around a yield point

questions.explanation: `@contextmanager` turns a generator into a context manager. Code before yield performs setup; code after yield performs cleanup, typically in a try/finally structure.

questions.question: Why might a generator be preferable to building a very large list?

options.text: It can process values incrementally without storing the entire result in memory
Generators always execute faster than lists

questions.explanation: Lazy iteration can reduce peak memory use for large data streams. It may not be faster in every workload and does not support ordinary random indexing.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `yield from`?

options.text: Yield a value from another thread
Delegate iteration to a sub-iterator or subgenerator
Return all values as a list

questions.explanation: `yield from` delegates iteration and generator control flow to a sub-iterator, including forwarding values and exceptions in generator contexts.

questions.question: What is a Python module?

options.text: A Python file that can define functions, classes, and variables

questions.explanation: A module is commonly a `.py` file that can be imported by other Python code.

questions.question: What is a Python package traditionally represented by?

options.text: A directory containing modules and commonly an `__init__.py` file

questions.explanation: Regular packages commonly contain `__init__.py`. Python also supports namespace packages that can span directories without that file.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `if __name__ == '__main__':`?

options.text: Run code only when the module is executed as the main program

questions.explanation: When a file is executed directly, its `__name__` is set to `__main__`. When imported, it is set to the module name.

questions.question: Why use a virtual environment for a Python project?

options.text: Make Python code run without an interpreter
Isolate project dependencies from other projects and the system Python environment

questions.explanation: Virtual environments provide an isolated installation context, helping projects use different dependency versions without interfering with one another.

questions.question: Which command commonly creates a virtual environment named `.venv`?
questions.explanation: `venv` is part of the Python standard library and is commonly invoked as a module.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `__init__.py` in a regular package?

options.text: It is always the application's entry point
It defines every class in the package
It marks the directory as a package and can contain package initialization code

questions.explanation: `__init__.py` can be empty or expose package-level names and initialization behavior. Namespace packages are an exception to the requirement.

questions.question: What is a circular import?

options.text: Two or more modules depend on each other through imports, potentially observing partially initialized modules
An import that downloads a package repeatedly
An import of a package with no functions
An import that uses a relative path

questions.explanation: Circular imports can occur when modules depend on each other during initialization. Refactoring shared definitions or moving imports to narrower scopes can help.

questions.question: What does `pip install -r requirements.txt` do?

options.text: Exports installed packages to a file
Installs packages listed in the requirements file

questions.explanation: `pip install -r` reads package requirements and installs them into the active environment.

questions.question: What is the benefit of pinning dependency versions?

options.text: It guarantees packages have no vulnerabilities
It improves reproducibility by controlling which package versions are installed

questions.explanation: Pinned or constrained versions reduce unexpected dependency drift. They do not guarantee security; dependency updates and vulnerability review remain necessary.

questions.question: What is the main difference between an absolute import and a relative import?

options.text: Absolute imports work only on Windows
Relative imports cannot import sibling modules
They are identical in all cases
An absolute import names a module from its package/import root; a relative import uses leading dots relative to the current package

questions.explanation: Absolute imports are explicit from the import root. Relative imports use dot notation to refer to the current package and its parents.

questions.question: What is an instance of a Python class?

options.text: A module imported by the class
An object created from that class
A decorator applied to a method

questions.explanation: A class defines behavior and structure; an instance is a concrete object created from it.

questions.question: What is the conventional first parameter name for an instance method?
questions.explanation: `self` refers to the current instance by convention. Python passes the instance automatically when an instance method is called through an object.

questions.question: Which method is commonly used to initialize a newly created instance?
questions.explanation: `__init__` initializes an instance after it has been created. Object creation itself is handled by `__new__`.

questions.question: What does inheritance allow a class to do?

options.text: Reuse and specialize behavior from a parent class
Convert instance attributes into global variables
Automatically persist itself to a database

questions.explanation: Inheritance models an is-a relationship and allows a subclass to extend or override parent behavior.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `super()`?

options.text: Call every method in the module
Access methods or behavior from the next class in the method resolution order

questions.explanation: `super()` provides a proxy for calling the next implementation in the MRO, which is especially important in cooperative multiple inheritance.

questions.question: What is the difference between a class variable and an instance variable?

options.text: A class variable is always private
An instance variable is shared by all objects
A class variable is shared through the class; an instance variable belongs to a particular object

questions.explanation: Class attributes are stored on the class and may be shared unless shadowed. Instance attributes are usually assigned through `self`.

questions.question: What does `@property` allow a class to define?

options.text: A method that can be accessed using attribute syntax
A static method that cannot access state
A class that cannot be instantiated
A method that always runs asynchronously

questions.explanation: `property` supports managed attributes with getter, setter, and deleter behavior while preserving attribute-style access.

questions.question: What is method overriding?

options.text: A subclass provides its own implementation of an inherited method
A class defines two variables with the same value

questions.explanation: Overriding lets a subclass customize inherited behavior while preserving a compatible method contract.

questions.question: What is composition in object-oriented design?

options.text: Making every class inherit from one base class
Copying all methods into each class
Building an object by combining or delegating to other objects

questions.explanation: Composition models has-a relationships and can reduce tight coupling compared with deep inheritance hierarchies.

questions.question: What does Python's method resolution order (MRO) determine?

options.text: The order in which modules are installed
The order in which object fields are serialized
The order in which threads execute
The order in which base classes are searched for attributes and methods

questions.explanation: Python uses C3 linearization to calculate an MRO, providing a consistent lookup order for multiple inheritance.

questions.question: What does Big-O notation describe?

options.text: The exact execution time on every computer
The number of Python modules imported
How an algorithm's resource use grows as input size grows
The memory address of an object

questions.explanation: Big-O expresses asymptotic growth, commonly for time or space complexity. It abstracts away machine-specific constant factors.

questions.question: What is the average-case time complexity of dictionary lookup by key?
questions.explanation: Dictionary lookup is average-case constant time under normal hashing assumptions, though worst-case behavior can degrade with collisions.

questions.question: Which tool is commonly used to measure execution time of small Python code snippets?
questions.explanation: `timeit` provides a repeatable way to time small snippets while reducing some measurement noise.

questions.question: What is profiling used for?

options.text: Automatically rewrite code in a faster language
Identify where a program spends time or other resources

questions.explanation: Profilers provide evidence about function call counts and execution time, helping focus optimization on actual bottlenecks.

questions.question: What does garbage collection help manage in Python?

options.text: Delete every variable at the end of each function
Reclaim memory used by objects that are no longer reachable, including cycles handled by cyclic GC

questions.explanation: CPython primarily uses reference counting and supplements it with cyclic garbage collection to handle reference cycles.

questions.question: Why can repeated string concatenation in a loop be inefficient?

options.text: Strings are mutable and cannot be concatenated
The loop always runs in parallel
The interpreter converts strings to files
It may repeatedly allocate and copy strings; joining collected parts is often more efficient

questions.explanation: Strings are immutable. Repeated concatenation can create many intermediate objects. Building a list and using `''.join(parts)` is often more efficient.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `__slots__` in a class?

options.text: Restrict allowed instance attributes and potentially reduce per-instance memory overhead
Prevent class inheritance in every case

questions.explanation: `__slots__` can avoid the usual per-instance `__dict__` and restrict dynamic attributes, but it has trade-offs involving inheritance, weak references, and flexibility.

questions.question: What is a common reason a Python program uses more memory than expected when processing a large file?

options.text: It reads or materializes the entire file or dataset instead of streaming it
It closes the file with a context manager

questions.explanation: Streaming line by line or processing chunks avoids retaining the entire dataset in memory.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `tracemalloc`?

options.text: Trace Python memory allocations to help investigate memory usage

questions.explanation: `tracemalloc` tracks Python memory allocations and can compare snapshots to identify allocation sources.

questions.question: Why should developers avoid optimizing code based only on intuition?

options.text: Python performance is always predictable from source length
The perceived bottleneck may not be the actual bottleneck, and changes can add complexity without measurable benefit

questions.explanation: Measure representative workloads first, identify the bottleneck, optimize the relevant part, and benchmark again to confirm improvement.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an assertion in a test?

options.text: Verify that an observed result matches an expected condition

questions.explanation: Assertions encode expected behavior. A failing assertion indicates that the test's expectation was not met.

questions.question: Which Python testing framework is included in the standard library?
questions.explanation: `unittest` is included with Python. Pytest is a widely used third-party framework with a concise fixture and assertion model.

questions.question: What is a fixture in pytest commonly used for?

options.text: Set up and provide reusable test dependencies or state

questions.explanation: Fixtures provide reusable setup and teardown for tests, such as temporary directories, clients, test data, or database sessions.

questions.question: What is mocking used for in unit tests?

options.text: Replace a dependency with a controlled test double

questions.explanation: Mocks and other test doubles isolate the unit under test from external systems and allow tests to verify interactions or simulate conditions.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a linter?

options.text: Detect potential issues and enforce code-quality rules

questions.explanation: Linters analyze source code for style issues, suspicious patterns, and potential bugs. Examples include Ruff and Pylint.

questions.question: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test?

options.text: A unit test always requires a database; an integration test never does
A unit test focuses on a small unit in isolation; an integration test checks interactions between components or systems
An integration test cannot use mocks

questions.explanation: Unit tests isolate a small piece of logic. Integration tests exercise boundaries such as repositories, HTTP layers, databases, or external integrations.

questions.question: Why should tests avoid depending on execution order?

options.text: pytest requires tests to run alphabetically
Order dependence creates hidden shared-state coupling and makes test runs less reliable

questions.explanation: Independent tests are easier to run in parallel, repeat, and debug. Shared mutable state should be isolated or reset between tests.

questions.question: What is test parametrization useful for?

options.text: Run the same test logic against multiple input and expected-output combinations

questions.explanation: Parametrization reduces duplication and makes edge-case coverage clearer by supplying multiple cases to one test function.

questions.question: What does code coverage measure?

options.text: Which parts of the code were executed during a test run
How fast the code runs in production
How many developers reviewed the code

questions.explanation: Coverage tools report executed lines, branches, or other units. High coverage does not guarantee that tests assert meaningful behavior.

questions.question: Why is a test that only asserts a mocked dependency was called sometimes insufficient?

options.text: Mocks cannot be used in Python
It may verify implementation details without proving the externally observable behavior is correct
A mock always executes the real implementation

questions.explanation: Interaction assertions can be valuable, but tests should also verify important outputs and behavior. Excessive mocking can make tests brittle and miss integration defects.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of Python type hints?

options.text: Enforce every type at runtime automatically
Document expected types and enable static analysis tools to detect potential type errors

questions.explanation: Type hints improve readability and tooling, but Python generally does not enforce them at runtime without additional validation tools.

questions.question: How do you annotate a function parameter as an integer?
questions.explanation: Python annotations use a colon after the parameter name. A return annotation follows `->`.

questions.question: What does `Optional[str]` traditionally mean in Python typing?

options.text: A value that can be a string or None
A string that may be empty only
A value that must be omitted

questions.explanation: `Optional[str]` is equivalent to `str | None` in modern Python versions that support union type syntax.

questions.question: What is a dataclass commonly used for?

options.text: Reducing boilerplate for classes primarily used to store structured data

questions.explanation: `@dataclass` can generate methods such as `__init__`, `__repr__`, and equality methods based on annotated fields.

questions.question: Which module provides the standard `Enum` base class?
questions.explanation: The `enum` module provides `Enum`, `IntEnum`, and related types for representing named constants.

questions.question: What is the difference between `list[int]` and `Sequence[int]` as type annotations?

options.text: `list[int]` is checked at runtime but `Sequence[int]` is not
They are interchangeable in all API contracts
`list[int]` describes a list specifically; `Sequence[int]` accepts a broader read-only sequence interface

questions.explanation: Use a concrete type when mutability or list-specific behavior is required. An abstract interface such as `Sequence` allows tuples and other sequence implementations.

questions.question: What is a `Protocol` in Python typing used for?

options.text: Define structural interfaces based on the operations an object provides
Create a network protocol implementation automatically
Enforce inheritance from a specific base class at runtime

questions.explanation: Protocols support structural subtyping: a type can satisfy a protocol by providing the required members without explicitly inheriting from it.

questions.question: What does `@dataclass(frozen=True)` provide?

options.text: A class that can never be instantiated
A dataclass with attribute assignment blocked after initialization
A class whose fields are all deleted after use
A class that is automatically persisted

questions.explanation: Frozen dataclasses emulate immutability by preventing ordinary attribute reassignment. They are not deeply immutable if fields reference mutable objects.

questions.question: What is a generic type variable useful for?

options.text: Expressing relationships between input and output types in reusable typed functions or classes

questions.explanation: Generics allow a function or class to preserve type relationships, such as returning the same type that was passed in.

questions.question: What is the difference between static typing and runtime validation?

options.text: Runtime validation only runs in the IDE
Static typing always validates JSON received over HTTP
Static typing analyzes code and annotations before execution; runtime validation checks actual values while the program runs

questions.explanation: Mypy, Pyright, and similar tools analyze type consistency statically. Runtime validators such as Pydantic inspect actual data values during execution.
